en: In former times, the illustrious Gautama Bodhisattva was the protector of those born as dogs.
He liberated his own circle of kinsmen from death and bestowed the gift of fearlessness upon the entire world.
Born in the lineage of that Bodhisattva of supreme virtue, this dog—
like a shadow, sharing my very state of standing and moving—
possesses a compassionate heart toward his lord and is worthy of praise by those who recognize their debts of gratitude.
May he live long, protecting the multitude of living beings with a joyful mind. ||2||
That dog, whom he had nourished with affection for his son by calling it with gentle words and giving it food and drink,
remained equal-minded toward both suffering and happiness and was grateful to him.
It never abandons its own master at any time whatsoever. ||3||
Beholding his protector, weak and afflicted by old age,
he yawned repeatedly as if overcome by grief;
the sound "bhuh-bhuh" was uttered by him in that moment of calamity.
She manifests her compassion toward her own husband. ||4||
Desiring to know whether his exhausted master— who was old, with impaired senses— was well and free from disease,
he wagged his tail and sniffed at his pair of feet.
And she utters the sound "kū-kū" very softly and repeatedly. ||5||
Having fallen down right in front of the leaf-hut, she protects her husband vigilantly throughout the night;
she rises, wanders about, and cries out for no apparent reason.
It constantly prevents the entry of wicked people. ||6||
Moving forward with focused intent toward his destination,
he seeks to drive far away the host of harmful beings;
he searches for a way to prevent the calamity that surrounds him.
Like a lion's cub, he roars with a long, drawn-out sound. ||7||
Even while asleep in a dilapidated hut made of wood, he finds no comfort in slumber as he guards his master;
thus he remains on his bed until the time of dawn.
And he wanders about at night, dejected and sleepless. ||8||
Having feigned sleep at dawn, he first awoke and repeatedly yawned to dispel his drowsiness; then,
drawing back the hem of the silk garment clinging to his master’s waist—
One should signal the end of the night with the cry "ku-ku-ru. ||9||
When the master, his body bent and leaning on a staff held in his hand, trembles like a plantain tree struck by the wind,
he makes a futile effort to walk as he stumbles heavily upon the path.
Even a dog would then be a superior companion and a kinsman. ||10||
A bold dog suddenly plunged into the lord who had fallen by chance into the current of the river,
and having dragged him out, pulled him to the bank with his cloth tied around his waist.
Having led [him] away, he once made him happy through his own labor. ||11||
Like a serpent coiled upon its body,
having perceived the approach of its master, it springs up with impetuosity;
it bows upward and then falls down again toward the Lord.
Embracing him, she kisses him and cries out with devotion. ||12||
The Lord, having once stumbled on the path, fell down unconscious with his eyes rolling and face turned upward;
crying out piteously and incessantly, "Amma! Amma! (O Mother! O Mother!)—he was thus addressed.
Furthermore, it turned repeatedly upward and downward. || 13 ||
In one place his staff, in another his alms-bowl, elsewhere his patched garment fastened at the waist,
and in yet another place his tattered rags with their heads covered in dust.
He cast [it] far away on every side along that path, here and there.
Now, no kinsman seeking his welfare has come to assist him, nor has any other person of benevolent intent;
only dogs wander here and there repeatedly around his body.
Wandering about on all sides, he embraced his own master. ||15||
Surrounded by that trembling body of his husband, he suddenly began to wander about, his chest afflicted by gasping breaths;
he cried out repeatedly with his head, his whole body [in distress].
He made a great effort merely to lift it up. ||16||
Then, desiring to offer some assistance to those facing him, he ran forward into the midst of the crowd,
raising his neck and head while keeping his tail steady.
He cried out repeatedly, for no one at all could perceive him.
Therefore, suddenly turning away, he seized his staff with his mouth and placed it near his master’s hand;
the master, too, grasping it with great difficulty, held it fast.
Having risen, he repeatedly stroked the head of the dog. ||18||
Indeed, neither I nor you were able, even after a long time, to wash clean that loathsome rag-robe, which was the dwelling place of vermin and possessed a foul odor.
O dog, do not attempt to kiss me now! (19)
Having tightly covered even his loincloth and head-cloth, and having placed his bowl in the palm of his hand,
with trembling feet and a bent upper body, he went forth.
Furthermore, this old man wanders again and again on the path of restless roaming. ||20||
Seeking alms, that hungry man stood at the courtyard of the mansion of a very wealthy man; then,
[the master] said, "Close your eyes and do not look at anything here as you go out."
The moneylender spoke to him contemptuously and with anger. ||21||
Therefore, having been dismissed by the wealthy man and hearing his harsh words,
the poor man, afflicted by grief, spoke thus to Śunaka: "O dog,
do not be dejected in any way."
Even a wealthy person, being stingy, does not wish to give anything away—alas!
I have no accumulated wealth, nor house, nor property; neither servants, nor attendants, nor mother, nor father.
My only possession is a loincloth, for I am destitute.
You alone are my kinsman, my son, my retinue, and my friend. ||23||
For a base enemy has indeed seized all his possessions;
today, my own state has become one of sheer wretchedness,
and my friends have turned away like enemies.
Indeed, for the sake of alms, I wander from there every day. ||24||
For me, afflicted by hunger, even the tasteless varieties of food obtained through wandering for alms become like nectar;
likewise, even a cracked vessel or a fragment of a worn-out skull [is sufficient].
My entire being is indeed [in him]; my dog alone is my kinsman. ||25||
An ignorant person, even when benefited by others with gold and jewels, corrupts his mind and devours well-nourished flesh;
for you have indeed been nourished by a regimen of meager food and drink.
A virtuous person becomes grateful, like a dog. ||26||
A wicked person, even if constantly served with a multitude of virtues,
can never in any way become a virtuous man; just as a tree,
though perpetually nourished by water and affection, [remains what it is].
Like a serpent, he is never satiated and can never be grateful. ||27||
It possesses two tongues, moves in a crooked manner, reveals its own openings, and destroys its benefactor;
it craves flesh and thirsts for blood.
Alas! What difference is there between a wicked person and a serpent? ||28||
These base beings, who are dear, devoted, and friendly when facing one, become great enemies and ungrateful when turned away;
they belong to the species of wicked, contemptible, deceitful, and evil men.
O dog, indeed your birth would be most excellent! ||29||
The moon dispels the darkness in the world with its rays everywhere and purifies the jasmine grove; you, by your very nature, dispel the darkness of sorrow in my heart.
You cause the white lotus of joy and delight to blossom fully. ||30||
Those friends who, like cuckoos dependent on others for their nourishment, forget a favor just as serpents do,
lead even their own life-force into calamity.
Like the vandārava tree among trees, they are to be completely shunned. ||31||
Those of wretched conduct, their minds overcome by craving, deceive the virtuous with various stratagems;
they offer feigned praise with sweet words.
Turning their faces away, they revile them with various kinds of idle chatter. ||32||
That person who does not return a favor done for him, though it was praised by wise and virtuous men,
is a wicked man devoid of human nature.
He goes to a state of ruin immediately after death. ||33||
With minds washed by the water of compassion for others, they seek to reach the state of heaven, the abode of bliss,
and desire to cross the ocean of birth, old age, and death.
They perform even greater acts of service for one who has previously rendered them assistance. ||34||
That miserly lowest of men who does not perform a service praised by those who have reached the further shore of all sciences and scriptures is a mere demon in human form.
That should be avoided like a lump of filth. ||35||
He who, having attained prosperity by receiving the instruction of a friend, forgets that kindness which is praised among the virtuous—
he is self-centered, wretched, and like a jackal in its old age.
It should be avoided like a corpse in a cremated cemetery. ||36||
Then that Prince Siddhārtha Gautama sat down beneath the Bodhi tree,
having utterly destroyed the hostile forces of Māra along with their very roots.
May he awaken to the state of supreme, great enlightenment. ||37||
After that, for seven days, the Lord of Sages,
gazing at the Bodhi tree with his pure eyes free from blinking, paid him worship.
He demonstrated his gratitude for the benefit bestowed upon the world. ||38||
If gratitude, which is the means for increasing both [merit and wealth] as taught by the Sage, does not exist in one's heart,
that person is a serpent moving about in human form.
This must be avoided by one who desires to attain the third heaven. ||39||
While her husband lay afflicted by disease at the side of his bed, the dogs struck their tails against the ground with piteous cries; then,
stretching their bodies upward, they remained with unblinking eyes.
Sitting down face-to-face, she utters the sound "kū-kū. ||40||
O son of a courtesan, O dog, do not grieve;
the meat you have eaten does not digest in your belly.
Today I am afflicted with cough, fever, and vomiting.
Neither medicine, nor attendants, nor even a physician [can help]. ||41||
Every limb of the body trembles,
its strength has vanished,
and pain persists within the joints of the bones.
Death has come close to me. ||42||
Just as those pierced by sharp arrows experience intense agony within their hearts,
even by the hosts of physicians in heaven.
For they can never be pacified. ||43||
Just as the piercing of a poisoned needle causes intense pain in the head,
so too does heavy sighing arise in particular.
It turns back the fury of the Ender like a swift wind. ||44||
His speech, unfinished and faltering, now emerges slowly from his mouth,
as the interior of his mouth and teeth have been wounded.
The rasanā functions as if it were inactive. ||45||
Now my hearing has been crushed by old age and sealed by death,
like the light of the moon when it has entered its waning phase.
The pair of eyes attains immortality. ||46||
O Suta, do not be afflicted by grief;
you are one who knows how to repay kindness among mortals born upon this earth.
I shall depart from you immediately.
Before long, I shall resort to the abode of Death. ||47||
The accumulation of your virtues has always been a mirror for mortal beings,
in order to instruct those who are ungrateful.
By you, you have become a bull among teachers. ||48||
Neither in the realm of the thirty-three gods nor on earth is there anything whatsoever that is permanent or eternal— so it was said by the Sage, the sole kinsman of the world.
Nirvāṇa itself is known to be perfectly stable. ||49||
"Among all beings, I am the most lowly of animals;
therefore, O friend dog, do not be despondent.
You have become praiseworthy for having performed a virtuous service."
And he has always protected me like a jewel held in the palm of his hand. ||50||
O wise and grateful dog, O best of dear friends,
may you never again take birth among human beings,
for your multitude of excellent virtues would not be surpassed even while they remain present.
May he live for a very long time in happiness for the benefit of the world. || 51 ||
The dog, having realized the truth, immediately ran to the presence of its master’s physician;
it licked his feet while gazing up at his face.
He quickly fell at his feet in a state of utter despondency. ||52||
The excellent physician did not perceive the dog's subtle gestures, nor did he take him into account; meanwhile,
the dog, overcome by grief, [sought] his own master once again.
Having repeatedly assumed a body, he kissed it all over.
Afflicted by an incurable disease, with impaired senses and ruined fortune, he departed this life and passed away to the next world;
yet, unable to endure separation from his master, oh, how grateful he was!
The dog tore open his heart and followed after him. ||54||

Born in this existence by the power of karma accumulated through *māyā*, amidst the ocean of suffering with its waves of death, birth, and old age— may I never again take birth among the wicked in the mortal world.
May there be for you only that Nirvana which is liberated from existence. //55//
The lordly ascetic Jñāneśvara, born in the village of Davuldeṇa,
composed this literary work known as *Śvānastava*.
